section.title: Stefan Mai: Manager Career Growth, Performance Systems, and Amazon vs Meta
section.deck: Stefan Mai, a former Meta senior manager and earlier Amazon engineer and manager, describes the manager transition, promotion politics, rating buckets and PIPs, and the cultural differences between Amazon and Meta.

blocks.text: Stefan Mai, who worked as an engineer and manager at Amazon and later reached senior manager (M2) at Meta, argues that managing well depends on small human behaviors: listening, telling a team its own story of winning, and understanding the personal incentives behind organizational politics. He also holds that no leadership style is best in the abstract, because what works depends on the stage and culture of the company. The host draws out his Amazon years, his move to Meta, promotions, rating buckets and PIPs, how AI is changing interviews, and his reflections on job hopping, writing and agency.
blocks.heading: Stefan Mai's view: management is trade-offs, and small behaviors and incentives decide outcomes

blocks.question: What did you work on at Amazon, and how did you get there?
answer: Stefan describes himself as an engineer who paid little attention to school and wanted to build. His early work was scattered across consulting and startups, and he felt he had not found technical depth. In 2012 Amazon offered work on hard problems at scale, and he took it despite the company's reputation for grinding engineers down. He joined the early advertising group, on a team building self-service advertising for vendors.

In his first week, he says, his manager gathered the team at about six in the evening and committed everyone to nights and weekends to ship by October, a death march of six to eight months. Stefan leaned in, though he says he would likely refuse today. The episode shaped his early development and his thinking about leading teams, and he calls it emblematic of the negative side of many people's Amazon experience.

followups.question: Did you choose advertising, or were you placed there?
answer: Amazon was not recruiting generally then. Candidates were approached for a specific organization, and Stefan's recruiter covered only advertising. He chose among several teams there, picking the one with the most growth, which he considers a good career choice because it was the start of Amazon's ad business.
followups.speaker: Stefan Mai

followups.question: Was the work always a grind, or only the early death march?
answer: The death march was not standard across his tenure. Stefan says the average was working hard, as any big-tech job demands, more so for the ambitious. Fifty to sixty hours a week was fairly common, though not always nights and weekends.
followups.speaker: Stefan Mai

blocks.speaker: Stefan Mai

blocks.question: Are there notable stories from your growth into a software development manager at Amazon?
answer: Stefan says his ownership meant he was often the de facto tech lead and effectively acted as the team's manager, because his boss had no time for the niceties managers normally provide. The title lagged what he felt he was doing, so he pushed for it.

He believes he got it prematurely. People feel ready, he says, without realizing how far they have to go. Most new managers make many early mistakes, and the support structure around them largely decides how they fare. His first year was uncomfortable and he was failing in ways he did not fully see. Around 18 months in he began to get a knack for it.

followups.question: What early mistakes made it premature?
answer: Stefan calls management a soft discipline with few output metrics, in which part of the job is telling the story of your contribution and of how you leveled people up. The soft skills were what he lacked. He had not learned each person's goals, and did not know how to get people to open up about what mattered most, so he could not tailor support or assignments to the individual. He calls that an elementary mistake.
followups.speaker: Stefan Mai

followups.question: Do you have tips for new managers on getting people to reveal their goals?
answer: Stefan says a new manager's position is tricky because the team knew them as a peer, and the new power dynamic corrodes those bonds. A manager needs to learn about career objectives and what in the current work drags on the person, not just whether a friend is having a good week.

His first advice is active listening, which engineers can take a while to learn: show interest, reflect back what was said so the person feels heard, and ask questions that show curiosity. Engineers often talk almost like APIs, he says, and most people are not like that. He adds that early on he ran one-on-ones as a transactional laundry list and thought opening small talk was wasted time. He now sees its value.
followups.speaker: Stefan Mai

blocks.speaker: Stefan Mai

blocks.question: Do you have tips for improving storytelling?
answer: Stefan calls storytelling a bedrock skill and says part of it is practice. People tell stories all the time without attending to them: recalling details is a story, and so is the motivation you give yourself to get out of bed. His first trick is to notice those moments and ask what story he is telling himself today, since one version helps you get up and another does not. Once you can critique your own stories, you can practice telling them better.

He says it came naturally to him as a manager. Every few months he looked back over what the team had accomplished and painted it clearly so people could feel proud, for example that they started as a team of two with a poor on-call, fixed it, and used the freed bandwidth to deliver.

Stefan's claim is that a team that feels it is winning, with the manager defining what winning means, gets much else downstream: people avoid zero-sum thinking and bickering, and feel excited about their work. Without that story, such problems fester.
blocks.speaker: Stefan Mai

blocks.question: What was your manager doing, and how did you get to do the manager's role before having the title?
answer: Stefan's manager was a senior manager expected to manage other managers but did not want to hire other SDMs, or wanted to delay as long as possible. Stefan's impression was that this was a way of keeping control of the product, which the manager loved: working with design and refining it for market. Stefan finds it debatable that this was the best use of the manager's time. Tasks a manager traditionally owns, such as checking progress, understanding careers and mentoring, fell by the wayside.

followups.question: Was the sentiment in that org negative?
answer: Stefan says a lot of people were pretty upset about the situation, and that he would not say things were particularly good.
followups.speaker: Stefan Mai

blocks.speaker: Stefan Mai

blocks.question: At the end of your Amazon stint, what made you leave and join Meta?
answer: Stefan first stresses that Amazon is a special and worthwhile place, undoubtedly successful and with a strong engineering discipline. His reasons for leaving built up after a considerable time there.

First, succeeding at Amazon involves assimilating into a distinctive leadership style the company called its peculiar ways. He came to feel that makes you a good Amazonian, not necessarily a good engineering leader, and he worried he was not growing. Second, Amazon keeps compensation more even, at some cost. He recalls a promotion or very high rating with no change to his compensation, explained by stock appreciation, which he found frustrating since it applied to the whole team.

Third, when a Facebook recruiter reached out, he was not a fan of the product but admired the engineering culture. The team was in integrity, working on child safety and preventing terrorism. At Amazon, his supply chain and ML work moved profitability, which had some effect on people but not the same qualitative impact. The first two reasons made him look, and this one tilted him into the move.

followups.question: Which parts of Amazon's peculiar ways suit Amazon but not engineering leadership in general?
answer: Stefan begins by saying all leadership is trade-offs and no style is best. Amazon's approach grew out of a company that long ran on low margins and operational leanness. Each management layer gets involved in detail in the layers beneath it, so even as a line manager he was expected to know what everyone on the team was doing at any moment.

The benefit is discipline: things do not just happen, and people track metrics closely. The cost is stifled creativity, which he did not see until he left. In his view it limits Amazon's ability to pursue new products while making it very effective in growth stages where the goal is to move revenue or cost by one percent.

He uses Kent Beck's explore, expand, extract framework. In explore, as at a seed-stage company, upside is asymmetric and moving fast matters. In extract, the best case is a one or two percent gain against a looming catastrophic risk, so risk aversion fits. Stefan finds Amazon's culture leans toward the later stages, partly because of how it has grown.
followups.speaker: Stefan Mai

blocks.speaker: Stefan Mai

blocks.question: How was the move into ML work and forecasting? Was it challenging?
answer: Stefan says it always is. Ordinary software projects are close to binary, working or not. ML is shades of gray, and people commonly carry bugs in a training pipeline for years without noticing, then fix them for marginally better performance. The work is scientific and experiment-driven, which was unfamiliar to him.

To make the move he read many books, entered Kaggle competitions, and built models on the side. Pivoting into AI is far more popular now, he notes, but many people treat it as a study session about learning the 101. The 101 matters, he says, but effectiveness also depends on judgment and instinct, which develop only by building and practicing.

followups.question: So the key was building intuition, not just learning the fundamentals?
answer: Stefan says for him the key was Kaggle plus finding ways to work ML into his existing role. Many things are non-obvious until you practice them.
followups.speaker: Stefan Mai

followups.question: What motivated the move into ML?
answer: Stefan always found ML interesting. Having coded from an early age by instructing computers step by step, he found it seductive that a program could be implied from data. Much of what mattered societally then, such as news-feed ranking, recommendations and Amazon's supply chain, was ML. In supply chain, machinery predicting truck arrivals, vendor inventory and customer demand combined to produce something forgettable, an item arriving at the door, and he finds the complexity behind that beautiful.
followups.speaker: Stefan Mai

blocks.speaker: Stefan Mai

blocks.question: What was the story behind your promotion from frontline manager to senior manager?
answer: Stefan was promoted about three and a half years into Meta, after roughly seven managers in that period. That turbulence held him back, and he suggests part of his promotion story is how to handle organizational shifts while keeping momentum.

On joining he wanted to be useful quickly, so he joined the on-call and wrote code, which built trust with his engineers and peer teams. That cannot be sustained, so he shifted to recruiting, where he says he had a blank check from his director. How people perceive a manager is a headwind or a tailwind, he says, and being pigeonholed can be devastating because people struggle to update their view of what someone will become.

Once his team's effectiveness was shown, he was given an additional manager. Leading a leader, he says, is yes and no the same as leading engineers: a far smaller shift than becoming a manager, but treating it as identical fails quickly, and for many it ends in mutiny. In manager stacks there is an unstated competition, since if the org is not growing, leaf-node managers can advance by taking the place of those they report to. His promotion came when his org reached about 30 to 40 people. By then he sat in calibrations alongside other M2s, and it was hard to deny he was doing the job.

followups.question: How does that mutiny surface in practice?
answer: Stefan says the easiest place to see it is skip-level meetings, where managers gripe that their manager is not helping, does not understand their career, or changes priorities too much. Some grumbling is about real problems, and some is a way to improve a manager's standing relative to their own boss.

He recounts a talk with his director about two teams in different organizations with overlapping responsibilities. Stefan saw a scientific experiment: let them run side by side and see who wins. The director called that naive, because the teams would find ways to undercut each other unrelated to their goal, and the friction would dwarf any gain. Stefan says the director was right. Most people have good intent, he adds, but want to move and grow in ways not always aligned with the organization, and a senior leader's job is to line those up.
followups.speaker: Stefan Mai

followups.question: Is there a secret chess, with personal career motives behind the business ones?
answer: Stefan would not call it secret, because it is fairly obvious. Few people's main objective is to make Facebook more valuable. Their goals are varied: money, positions or influence, interesting problems, working with certain people.

His examples, around an interesting project, are to pair up and form a coalition, cookie-lick by being first to put a name on it, announce it in a post so it is hard to pull someone away, or show others are not capable. Being aware of that dimension is, in his view, key to being a senior leader of any large organization.
followups.speaker: Stefan Mai

followups.question: Is this zero-sum behavior more common in shrinking or stagnant orgs, with growth bringing abundance?
answer: Stefan agrees. The zero-sum mentality usually appears when winning slows: the org stops growing, success is less obvious, and people redefine it. A leader's job is to equip the team to win, and focus on performance is among the most fundamental, with many other problems downstream. He adds that different leadership styles fit different stages. Early Facebook leaders were talented engineering leaders who rode a wave of growth, and whether the same people do best during a plateau is, he says, an open question.
followups.speaker: Stefan Mai

followups.question: So the mutiny is a manager telling their skip-level boss that you are thrashing things?
answer: Stefan says it looks like any disgruntled team: people make noise because they are unhappy, and the implicit goal is a change, most obviously of people. He adds that seniority reduces control over outcomes. A senior leader whose manager underperforms cannot do that job for them without the manager hating it and leaving. The higher you go, the more impact on direct reports shrinks and the more action becomes binary. There are fewer levers to turn things around.
followups.speaker: Stefan Mai

blocks.speaker: Stefan Mai

blocks.question: Are managers harder to lay off than ICs?
answer: Stefan says moving managers is inherently painful because the blast radius is larger. Whether removal is hard depends on whether the person is load-bearing: someone with a tight team and deep domain knowledge, whose cross-functional partners are not pulling their weight, is very hard to move out. If the team sees little value and partners complain, removal can even be invigorating.

On layoffs, he does not think managers are less likely to be cut. Most companies target a ratio of managers to ICs, so after cutting many ICs they need fewer managers. Companies also do span-of-control reductions, which he believes Amazon did recently, and managers go first. He does not think it is easier or harder for a comparably leveled IC.
blocks.speaker: Stefan Mai

blocks.question: What leadership is most effective in a very small company versus a very big one?
answer: Stefan says small companies need inspirational executors. Work is all hands on deck, and people want to work for someone impressive who could do their job and step in. As companies scale this gets harder, and those same people often lack the organizational aptitude needed. In big companies, he says, focus is a precious commodity. Go-getters who run at an opportunity without aligning or moving information up and down the chart get in the way and siphon energy from core initiatives.

He contrasts how Amazon and Meta scaled. Amazon built concrete API-like boundaries between teams, each owning two or three metrics, so leaders could assemble dependable pieces into a tall stack. The cost was value lost in organizational seams and slow response to change. Facebook's org was malleable: engineers moved between projects, assignments were weak, and code was communally owned. Its leaders needed soft alignment skills, knowing people's strengths and how to move and inspire them.

Stefan adds a caveat: a company cannot be staffed only with organizationally savvy people, since it turns negative-sum, with sharks fighting each other. As an example he offers OpenAI, noting he has not worked there and is relying on its hiring process and conversations with people inside. Its interviews favor technical achievements over organizational skill. It has plenty of politics, he says, but in its early phase it needs technical achievers to attract talent. As orgs grow there is entropy, and a need for people who can navigate it.
blocks.speaker: Stefan Mai

blocks.question: If a typical M1 were dropped into an M2 role, what would be the biggest skill gaps?
answer: Stefan says the main gap is credibly adding value to the people who report to you. Managers of managers have fewer ways to interact with teams, and a straight M1 struggles to recognize those limits and where to use the important ones.

His illustration is a new M1 who sets up skip-levels and asks an indirect report, Jan, leading questions about whether her manager, Jim, is doing the job. Jim confronts the M1 a week later, and Jan says the M1 has insights Jim lacked. The M1 has disintermediated Jim, demotivated Jan and created new problems. Small acts by a senior leader have magnification effects, he says, and you learn them by observing or by having a good model of how things propagate.

Such mistakes are the easy way for a new M1 to fail, and he says leadership expects them, as with a first-time manager. Strategy and org design mistakes come later, but small behavioral ones in the first weeks can sink you.
blocks.speaker: Stefan Mai

blocks.question: How do IC and management growth paths compare, and are both meritocratic?
answer: Stefan says at high levels everything becomes opaque and fuzzy. In calibrations he found it hard to stomach very senior ICs talking a big game without visible evidence, since it was unclear whether they were merely around valuable initiatives or instrumental in driving them. The same goes for managers: attribution is hard. Over a long run, such as four years of continued success in a role, it is undeniable, but on a half-to-half basis it is dubious.

For ICs at the sixes and maybe sevens, an outside observer can tell more easily, and an M1's team and deliverables allow a decent read. Further up, someone outside the leadership chain cannot see as clearly, and Stefan sees some unaccountability in much of management, comparable to judging a company's leadership team in the stock market. At some level, he says, it is difficult to have the data. The host summarized this as early promotions being easiest to verify and later ones more open to optics and narratives, and Stefan said that was a good summary.
blocks.speaker: Stefan Mai

blocks.question: What cultural differences stand out between Meta and Amazon?
answer: Stefan says Amazon is disciplined, a major strength, and he would expect more structured design reviews there. He thinks Meta engineers were on average a bit stronger but less disciplined, so reviews were fuzzier. Amazon was more predictable, partly because the business moves slower and partly because you can rely on other teams to meet SLAs. At Meta you might have to make the change yourself because the owner now works on photos. Many who move from Amazon to Meta find the unstructured environment paralyzing.

At Meta, the main positive he saw was openness and collaboration: engineers on his team worked with orgs across the company, such as a researcher in Paris, often without him setting it up. He also liked Meta's focus on empowering people. Amazon is process-oriented: when something fails, it adds a mechanism to prevent a repeat, whereas at Meta someone is more likely to say they learned the lesson. That has downsides, he says, and many of Facebook's privacy issues reflect an inability to do the process work Amazon does well. In ML, he was surprised by how hard data access was at Amazon, with teams building their own data lakes, while Meta had one shared warehouse.

Stefan prefers Meta's approach, especially for leadership, but missed some things from Amazon. For some people, he thinks Amazon is the better fit, since they would like it more than Meta's chaotic execution.
blocks.speaker: Stefan Mai

blocks.question: How do the performance systems at Meta and Amazon compare?
answer: Stefan says they are pretty close. There is a public process in which ratings are set and given to reports, and a more private process, usually limited to higher levels, to decide where to invest: a top-tier designation at Amazon, additional or discretionary equity at Meta. The aim is to find the linchpins the company wants to keep. Whichever company, people must believe the process rewards performance.

He once tracked the time spent on Meta's review cycle (PSC) and estimated the cost at about $15,000 per engineer. The tempting reaction is that this is wasteful, but he says that misses the forest for the trees: the integrity of the review process is the whole ballgame, and if people do not believe it produces outcomes for them, they will not perform.

One difference he saw is that Meta was willing to go to bat for the upper quintile. Amazon, partly from frugality and partly from fairness, did less of this. In his org some engineers received about twice as much compensation as peers through extra equity, because they were seen as very important and going places. At Amazon that is uncommon, and the company tends to find a way to pull it back.

followups.question: How do conversations about discretionary equity or top tier work?
answer: Stefan says VPs and directors usually drive it, and how much they involve managers varies. Being asked who deserves it is a sign of trust. The question is who has trajectory, the rocket ship, even after a stellar but not exceptional half. At Amazon he recalls growth and replaceability, meaning whether the person's leaving would break the organization, as the two dimensions. Those positions can be lucrative, since companies tighten golden handcuffs when the org depends on someone.
followups.speaker: Stefan Mai

blocks.speaker: Stefan Mai

blocks.question: Did you experience low-performer quotas, and how do they work?
answer: Stefan says every company of scale has them. In Meta's PSC process a merely good half gets written up as world-shaking, and assessments inflate in a way that cannot be true on average. Companies therefore target a distribution and, to keep performance high, must let some people go. Managers dislike this, Stefan included, but if a team does not act on a low performer, the team suffers because it no longer seems fair.

He says the share placed in the lower bucket varies, typically seven to 15 percent and sometimes up to 20, called needs improvement at Amazon and, per the captions, meets some or meets most at Meta. Some in that bucket are expected not to make the cut, and that is when PIPs start. Managers fight to keep people out, mostly to save face.

The worst scenario, he says, is telling a team how hard they have worked, then being told by your director that someone must be in the low bucket, and having to tell that person their work was not acceptable. A better case is a manager who messages a lower-quartile outcome early, so nobody is surprised.

followups.question: Do PIPs work, or are they a formality to create a paper trail? Do they differ between companies?
answer: Stefan says people can definitely get out of a PIP. It is first and foremost a legal paper trail, but to keep that credible people must be able to get through it. HR usually moderates, and its appetite to advocate for the employee varies.

At Amazon, while he was there, HR mainly wanted managers to check the boxes, and he calls it a pretty savage culture. Expectations are set, and the employee either turns it around or is gone, with managers holding a lot of discretion. Since most managers dislike firing, a manager may genuinely be rooting for the employee, though whether their hands are tied is up to some other power.

At Meta, he says, HR wanted every avenue exhausted before letting someone go. This is probably not true of modern Meta, but it was several years back, partly to protect its reputation as an employer. Stefan says this sounds cold, but companies have to reward performance, so terminations are part of the picture. They should be handled fairly and sensitively, but they have to happen or the company will not last long.
followups.speaker: Stefan Mai

blocks.speaker: Stefan Mai

blocks.question: With AI cheating tools and LLM assistants, how much does cheating come up in interview prep?
answer: Stefan says incentives in interview prep are mostly aligned, so cheating at mock interviews makes little sense, yet it has happened a few times. A coach reported a candidate talking to a friend in the background. His guess is that candidates may be testing their setup.

Remote interviews have always been somewhat cheatable, he says, and current tools make it worse. Recruiting teams over-rely on mechanisms that probably are not fully effective, such as checking browser focus or copy-paste activity, which catch only the least sophisticated. He expects interviews to change because software engineering is changing, with some companies allowing AI in assignments or choosing questions AI routinely gets wrong. He is more optimistic about evolving assessments than about anti-cheat measures.

He adds that companies are ruthless about performance now, so someone who cheats into a job may find it does not pan out. He has no formal accounting, but says plenty of people find themselves on the rough side of a review shortly afterward.

followups.question: Algo interviews seem easier to cheat on than system design. Do you see a shift?
answer: Stefan says companies are leaning more into design interviews, including lower-level design: classes, coupling and interactions between subsystems. In an AI-coded world, he says, the quality of design is load-bearing, and good abstractions matter more.

He has not seen any acute departure from coding interviews. People have predicted the demise of LeetCode for ages, but it serves a useful purpose for companies. Interviewing is very painful, but he thinks calling it broken goes too far, and it is premature to assume coding rounds will go away in the short to mid term.
followups.speaker: Stefan Mai

blocks.speaker: Stefan Mai

blocks.question: If someone were set on passing OpenAI or Anthropic interviews, what is the optimal game plan?
answer: Stefan says it varies, but those companies look for depth. OpenAI was notorious for asking the same questions in basically every interview, and he does not know why. Going deep on the functional areas they tended to ask about was an effective preparation strategy. That is not memorizing solutions, since interviewers are cleverer than that, but knowing roughly the areas gives a step up.

Behavioral and retrospective interviews matter a lot there, he says, because the companies want to see whether candidates have walked the walk. Because that is hard to judge yourself, he suggests asking a friend how you came across. He repeats his point about leaning toward technical accomplishments, not how you massaged the organization. For many people, he says, the crowning achievement of a big-tech staff career is seven docs, six teams aligned and five lines of code. That work was hard, but these companies do not value it the same way.
blocks.speaker: Stefan Mai

blocks.question: What are your thoughts on job hopping, given you stayed in roles for around four years?
answer: Stefan says that for ambitious people at lower levels, moving usually has advantages, because growth tends to come when you are uncomfortable in a new environment and must generalize your skills. He has not subscribed to it himself, since his motivation is going deep: after about two years he reaches the point where he can make an impact, which he finds most rewarding.

At higher levels, he says, frequent moves are a bad sign, because it is hard to get deep enough to build relationships and understand the domain. As a hiring manager he would second-guess a senior person moving every 18 months or two years, since he would invest a year ramping them up and then see them leave. For a mid-level hire that is a decent tenure, but for staff level he would hesitate. Early on, moving makes sense; as you get more senior, it pays to find places to put down roots.

followups.question: The host suggests credibility compounds like a snowball inside one org, which is why hopping helps less later. Does that fit?
answer: Stefan adds a trap: the snowball can become a shackle. Some very senior engineers become known for the system they created, and however hard they try to move in new directions, everyone knows them for that thing and they are stuck. He suggests asking yourself how comfortable you are. If you are not challenged, even at a senior level, it may be time to move. Otherwise the snowball works in your favor.
followups.speaker: Stefan Mai

blocks.speaker: Stefan Mai

blocks.question: Looking across your career, when did you grow the most, and why?
answer: Stefan says mostly at transitions, when he is in a new space learning and applying at once, which stress-tests his skills and shows what is durable and what was fake. Moving to Facebook stretched him, from a leadership perspective, in unexpected ways amid a lot of stress in the company. The pivot into an ML-focused role left him feeling he had a lot to prove, which brought external pressure he appreciated.

Other growth happens over smaller spans. A lot of his effectiveness as an IC and manager comes from writing well, which he largely learned at Amazon. He says some of Amazon's writing culture is a waste of time, with people nitpicking trivia, but the company encourages good writing, which means good thinking at some level.

followups.question: What is your top tip for an IC or EM who needs to improve their writing?
answer: Stefan's main tip is to learn to be a critic first. Work out what you like and dislike in writing: read a doc, notice what hits you, scan it to see whether you get the big picture in seconds, and look for imprecision or conclusions that are not well supported.

When he first wrote docs at Amazon he got a lot of negative feedback while thinking they were great. He cites Amazon's PR FAQ exercise, a press release followed by frequently asked questions: fast-forward to the end and get the reader excited about what will be delivered, and if you cannot sell it there, it probably was not worth doing. Many PR FAQs open with a single pane of glass, which excites nobody, whereas people respond to something like a 50 percent reduction in time spent. Admitting your own writing is boring to anyone not knee-deep in it is, he says, the first step to good writing. The host summarized this as honing your taste as a reader first, and Stefan added: then practice.
followups.speaker: Stefan Mai

blocks.speaker: Stefan Mai

blocks.question: What motivates you now, having left for a startup after so much success at Meta?
answer: Stefan says he likes interesting problems, ones he can tell his kids about and that set the stage for the future. The relentless march up the ladder is secondary for him now. Money matters because it powers everything, he says, but he realized he might be near the cap of what he could achieve in the ranks and asked what came next.

His method is to ask that question and then work backwards: if you want that thing, why not now, and what is keeping you? For more than a decade his answer was that he wanted to start a business, and he gave himself excuses. Eventually he told himself he was lying to himself. That was the impetus to leave big tech and build a business, and asking what he is really after remains his animating force.
blocks.speaker: Stefan Mai

blocks.question: If you could advise yourself just after college, what would you say?
answer: Stefan says he could have been better about finding mentorship. He did much of it alone, and asking someone like himself three questions might have saved months of toil.

He also points to written plans: taking stock of where he was, deciding where he wanted to go, and building a checklist. He still has an old plan in his Dropbox for getting into ML. Such plans paid incredible dividends that he still under-emphasizes. Most people lack the agency to decide where they want to go and then take it, but the world is very malleable to such plans.

He recalls that shortly after becoming a senior manager he told his boss and director a long list of things he would get done, many of which he did not know how to do. The director later told him that this was the moment he knew Stefan would succeed in the role. Lack of agency holds many people back and is hard to instill, Stefan says, but forcing yourself to write a plan for what you really want has a huge gradient on your ability to grow.
blocks.speaker: Stefan Mai
